newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO set to deploy half Bosnia peace force in 1997.
newsitem.headline: NATO set to deploy half Bosnia peace force in 1997.

text.p: The NATO-led peacekeeping operation in Bosnia next year looks likely to be down about half, involving 25,000 to 30,000 troops, informed sources said on Monday.
A decision on the force's makeup will be made next week.

"A consensus has already begun to emerge," said a NATO official after the North Atlantic Council (NAC),the alliance's political wing, reviewed options for when the current force mandate expires on December 20.
NATO members have been asked to examine four proposals -- ranging from total withdrawal of troops to leaving the entire near-60,000 force in place -- and to report back on November 18.

The official told Reuters that, while not all of the 16 alliance members committed themselves verbally on Monday to back continuation of the Peace Implementation Force in Yugoslavia (IFOR), "no one said they would oppose it either."
The direction the so-called "post-IFOR force" is most likely to take centres on two options which favour a gradual reduction in troop strength over the next 12 months.
The first, favoured by NATO military chiefs, would see IFOR reduced by about half with a substantial "crack force" based locally to prevent and deter any renewed conflict.

The second, preferred by politicians, calls for a similar reduction but with a rapid reaction force based outside Bosnia. Troops in the country would instead concentrate their efforts on stabilisation and reconstruction.
"The final version will be somewhere between these two," one NATO diplomat told Reuters earlier. "The other options (withdrawal or status quo) are the unlikely versus the undesirable."
IFOR was set up last year to police the U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accord which brought a fragile truce after years of conflict in the former Yugoslavia.
At its peak it numbered over 60,000 troops from 33 nations and included soldiers from former Cold War foes working together.
Government leaders from many contributing nations have made no secret of their desire to get out sooner rather than later when the IFOR mandate expires.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and his Republican election opponent Bob Dole were careful not to make any commitment to the IFOR force during their campaigns for fear of alienating voters.
But NATO diplomats hope that with the security of a further four years in office, Clinton will now be prepared to commit American troops to the next stage of the effort.
"The U.S. election has lifted a big cloud on the future of the force," said one diplomat, "but it is still important that we let the Bosnians know we do not want to be around forever."
"If we don't have a measured, careful, next 12 months all the work of the previous year will be in vain," said one diplomat.
